title: How We Scaled Ligerio to €10M Revenue — Operations, Logistics and Systems in a 2.5-Tonne Average Order Business
excerpt: Ligerio sells heavy flooring and wall coverings online — average order weight: 2.5 tonnes, delivered on pallets by 19-tonne trucks. We scaled from near-zero to €10M+ revenue in 4 years with 50–100% YoY growth, reached break-even in March 2024, and achieved 20x logistics throughput without proportional headcount growth. Here is the full operations story.
content:
# How We Scaled Ligerio to €10M Revenue — Operations, Logistics and Systems in a 2.5-Tonne Average Order Business

Selling flooring and wall coverings online sounds simple until you realise the average order weighs 2.5 tonnes. This is not a book or a T-shirt. It is one or several pallets moving from a supplier warehouse to a private home, an apartment renovation, or a professional construction site — requiring a 19-tonne truck, a liftgate, an advance appointment, and a carrier who understands that the customer cannot receive their delivery on a random Tuesday with 10 minutes of notice.

I joined Ligerio as co-founder in 2021, when Jean de Varine — whom I had met years earlier at Rocket Internet in West Africa — was already building the foundation. Over four years, we scaled from near-zero to €10M+ in annual revenue, achieving 50–100% year-on-year growth for three consecutive years. We reached break-even in March 2024. We built a team of 40+. We raised €3.9M. And we exited in mid-2025.

This is not a fundraising story. It is an operations story.

---

## The market: large, fragmented, and almost entirely offline

The French renovation and interior decoration market is estimated at €13 billion. The flooring segment alone represents approximately €4 billion annually in France — and most of it is still sold in physical stores: specialist flooring shops, DIY chains, trade wholesalers. Buying quality flooring online remains genuinely difficult: the products are heavy, bulky, expensive, and require expertise to select correctly. Customers need to match formats, quantities, technical specifications, and finishes — often across multiple suppliers.

In Europe, the flooring market is projected to grow at approximately 4.65% CAGR between 2024 and 2029, driven by renovation activity and rising demand for premium materials. Yet digital penetration remains low. The opportunity Ligerio identified was structural: build a proper online destination with better content, better UX, and — critically — logistics infrastructure that could actually deliver heavy products reliably to private individuals and professionals.

The thesis was right. The execution was hard.

---

## MVP: a Wix site with 10 references and a dropshipping model

The early version of Ligerio was intentionally minimal. A simple website, a limited catalogue, dropshipping as the supply model. This was the correct first step: before investing in infrastructure, you need to understand what customers actually buy, how they buy it, and where the friction is. In dropshipping, the supplier ships directly to the customer. Your upfront working capital is zero. You test demand without committing to stock.

For heavy goods, this matters particularly. Holding inventory in flooring means committing capital to products that weigh tonnes, take up significant warehouse space, and can take weeks to move. Getting the demand signal right before building supply capacity is not optional — it is a necessity.

Dropshipping gross margins in e-commerce typically run 15–30% — significantly below the 40–60% achievable with held inventory. But the capital efficiency justifies the margin trade-off in the early phase: you validate the market without the risk of expensive dead stock.

The ceiling hits fast. When volume grows, suppliers' logistics capacity — designed for B2B freight, not B2C e-commerce — becomes the binding constraint. Lead times vary, tracking is opaque, delivery quality is inconsistent. You are entirely dependent on how well your suppliers happen to be organised.

---

## The real constraint: B2C pallet logistics at scale

In most e-commerce, last-mile delivery is a cost to optimise. In heavy-goods e-commerce, last-mile delivery is the product experience. A customer who has ordered 40m² of stone flooring for a renovation project is not buying tiles — they are buying the certainty that the right product will arrive intact, on time, at the right address.

The logistics reality at Ligerio was specific:

- Orders over 30kg ship on pallets
- Standard delivery uses 19-tonne trucks with liftgate for pallet offloading
- Urban or access-constrained deliveries require smaller 20m³ trucks with embedded forklifts
- Appointment scheduling is required: carriers contact customers 24–72h before delivery
- The customer must be present and the address must be accessible to heavy vehicles

This is operationally incomparable to parcel delivery. There is no standard courier service for a 600kg stone pallet. The carriers who can manage this reliably — appointment-based, liftgate-equipped, capable of navigating construction site access — are specialised, fewer in number, and more expensive. Finding and building relationships with the right carrier network was itself a competitive advantage.

We worked with [Clic Logistic](http://www.clic-logistic.com/case_study/ligerio/) as our specialist logistics partner, selected specifically for their ability to handle out-of-gauge freight at scale. As Jean de Varine described publicly: "We have a huge volume of out-of-gauge products, and their ability to manage them — both in storage and in B2C delivery — is a complex service for a logistics provider."

The last-mile cost structure for heavy goods differs structurally from parcel economics. Hidden costs compound rapidly: damage and return rates are expensive (damaged stone flooring is not a €15 parcel — it is a €500+ order plus return logistics and reshipment), appointment rescheduling creates cascading delays, residential surcharges and detention fees erode margin. Building clean operational processes around these variables — supplier pallet preparation standards, carrier briefing protocols, customer communication sequences — was the prerequisite for everything else.

---

## The supply model shift: dropshipping → consignment → own stock

The model evolution that drove our margin improvement and operational control was a deliberate, data-driven segmentation of our supply model by product velocity.

**Consignment** sits between dropshipping and full stock ownership. The supplier delivers inventory to Ligerio's warehouse. That inventory remains the supplier's property until it is sold — we pay nothing upfront for unsold goods, and ownership only transfers at point of sale. Consignment requires zero upfront capital (unlike standard stocking) while giving us full control over picking, packing, and delivery timing.

The economics are significant. Where dropshipping delivers 15–30% gross margins, consignment and self-stocking typically yield 40–60% — a spread that compounds at €10M in revenue. On our top-selling references, the margin difference between dropshipping and consignment represented hundreds of thousands of euros in annual gross profit.

The discipline we applied was velocity-based segmentation:

- **New or unproven references**: tested in dropshipping first. Zero capital commitment. The velocity data decides.
- **Proven best-sellers with reliable demand**: moved to consignment. We control quality and speed; the supplier bears inventory risk.
- **High-volume core references**: progressively moved to own stock. Maximum margin, maximum delivery speed.

As we described in the [Le Panier podcast #286](https://lepanier.io/10m-de-ca-en-5-ans-en-vendant-des-materiaux-de-construction/): "You do not go on an adventure when you are immobilising stock for months — you do it on products you already understand." This principle sounds obvious. In practice, most e-commerce businesses apply one supply model uniformly across their entire catalogue and leave significant margin on the table.

The accounting treatment is also worth noting: consigned inventory does not appear on your balance sheet under French or international accounting standards. You are holding someone else's property. This keeps working capital requirements low while improving the economics of delivery, which is the critical variable in heavy-goods e-commerce.

---

## Scaling throughput 20x without proportional headcount growth

The single operational metric I am most proud of at Ligerio is not the revenue figure. It is the logistics throughput improvement over three years: we multiplied the volume of orders processed, coordinated and shipped by 20x — without a proportional increase in operational headcount.

This is the core challenge that every e-commerce operation hits between €2M and €5M in revenue. Operations researchers consistently identify this as the "fulfillment wall": the point at which manual coordination becomes the binding constraint on growth. You can hire through it — or you can build systems through it.

We built systems. Four levers worked in combination:

**1. Supplier interface standardisation.** Manual communication with suppliers — phone calls, emails, scattered formats — does not scale. We built structured supplier processes: standardised order formats, systematic status update protocols, clear escalation paths for exceptions. Every supplier interaction that required a phone call was a process failure to investigate. The goal was to transform supplier coordination from a reactive, manual activity into a structured, automatable flow.

**2. Carrier specialisation and relationship building.** B2C pallet delivery is a niche that most carriers are not built for. We invested in identifying and qualifying carriers who specifically understood residential freight: appointment scheduling, liftgate operation, access constraints, the specific handling requirements of fragile stone and ceramic tiles. This reduced damage rates — which in heavy goods directly impacts return logistics costs and customer experience — and delivery failures, which in renovation contexts can derail a contractor's schedule.

**3. Process documentation and playbook-driven operations.** Every exception that happened once was treated as a process design signal. We documented it, built a resolution protocol, and turned it into a playbook. The goal was to remove dependency on institutional memory: any team member should be able to handle a supplier dispute, a delivery failure, or a damaged pallet claim without escalating. This is the difference between a five-person ops team that scales and a five-person team that is permanently at capacity.

**4. Pragmatic tooling for end-to-end visibility.** Not custom-built software — the right tool choices to give real-time visibility across the full order lifecycle (order status, stock levels, carrier tracking, supplier confirmations) without requiring manual data entry at each step. The default state of the system was visibility; exceptions surfaced automatically rather than being discovered when a customer complained.

Collectively, these levers allowed a small operational team to manage a volume that would have required a much larger headcount in a traditional manual-coordination model.

---

## SEO as an operating function, not a marketing campaign

Our primary acquisition channel was organic search — and our approach to it was deliberately operational rather than campaign-based.

We built what we called a "war room" approach to SEO: a systematic, process-driven content production operation combining editorial judgment with AI-assisted production. The ambition was to become the most useful destination on the French web for anyone planning a renovation involving flooring or wall coverings — not by maximising content volume, but by genuine usefulness at each stage of the purchase journey.

The methodology had clear structure:

**Intent mapping before production.** Before publishing any content, we mapped the actual questions buyers ask at each purchase stage — from initial inspiration ("what flooring works in a wet bathroom?") to specification ("how many tiles for 25m²?") to purchase intent ("best price for Burgundy stone tiles"). Content was planned around buyer intent, not keyword lists.

**Content clusters, not isolated pages.** We built thematic clusters: a main category page supported by a constellation of supporting articles, buyer guides, and technical FAQ content. Topical authority at cluster level outperforms isolated pages in organic search — search engines increasingly reward depth within a topic rather than breadth across disconnected pages.

**AI-assisted production with human editorial oversight.** Scaling content production without quality decay requires genuine process discipline. We used AI-assisted drafting for high-volume informational content, with human editorial review for technical accuracy, brand tone, and conversion relevance. At 100k+ monthly organic clicks, SEO is an operational system — it cannot be run with a freelancer and a spreadsheet.

**Performance tracking by cluster and buyer stage.** We measured by content cluster and buying-stage conversion, not by individual page traffic. Informational content that drives traffic but never reaches product pages is a different diagnostic problem from category pages with high intent and low conversion rate.

The results: 200,000+ monthly website visitors, €400k/year in total acquisition budget, and 100k+ organic clicks as a sustained baseline. For a business where purchase cycles are long and average order values are high — someone planning a full renovation takes time before buying — organic search delivers structurally superior economics to paid acquisition: the traffic compounds, it does not stop when the budget does.

---

## The B2B channel: a market signal we listened to

Ligerio launched as a B2C brand. Within two years, approximately 40% of our customers were professionals — architects, interior designers, renovation contractors, and building artisans buying in volume for client projects.

This was not a planned pivot. It was a market signal. Professionals found us because the product quality, catalogue breadth, and logistical reliability were better than what most trade distributors offered. When a significant fraction of your revenue is coming from a customer segment you were not targeting, the right response is not to redirect them — it is to build deliberately for them.

We built a dedicated professional channel: trade pricing (ex-VAT), dedicated account management, delivery coordination adapted for construction site constraints, and eventually a separate platform designed for professional purchase workflows.

The operational challenge is that B2B and B2C have different requirement profiles: a professional artisan needs confirmed delivery dates (a renovation calendar has dependencies), a different invoicing structure, and different return conditions. Serving both segments from the same infrastructure requires deliberate separation at the service layer while keeping the catalogue, logistics, and CRM unified — otherwise you optimise for neither.

---

## Funding and break-even: the milestone that actually mattered

In November 2022, we closed a [€3.9M seed round](https://www.frenchweb.fr/seed-e-commerce-ligerio-leve-39-millions-deuros-aupres-de-go-capital-et-de-business-angels/437388) with Go Capital (Loire Valley Invest), BPI France, and business angels including Sébastien de Lafond (founder of MeilleursAgents), the Deconinck family (Tarkett), Clément Ouizille (Convelio), and Folco Aloisi (Karavel group).

The strategic rationale was catalogue expansion, technology investment, and B2B channel development. The ambition stated at the time was €50M in annual revenue with 10,000+ product references.

The milestone that actually mattered operationally was March 2024: break-even. In a macro environment where e-commerce unit economics were under pressure — rising acquisition costs, freight costs, return rates — reaching break-even on a first seed round validates the operating model. It means the business generates enough gross margin to cover its cost base at current scale. That is a proof of concept for the unit economics before raising further capital to accelerate.

---

## What Ligerio taught me about operations

Four years in heavy-goods e-commerce left me with convictions I carry into every subsequent project.

**Constraint is a forcing function for systems thinking.** The 2.5-tonne average order was not a handicap — it was the reason we built real operational infrastructure. Businesses that face genuinely hard logistics constraints tend to build better operations than those where logistics is easy. Difficulty forces discipline.

**The fulfillment wall is a systems problem, not a headcount problem.** The standard response to volume growth is hiring. The better response is identifying which parts of the operation are manual, why they are manual, and whether they need to be. The 20x throughput improvement at Ligerio came from asking that question systematically — not from doubling the team.

**Supply model segmentation by velocity is a genuine competitive lever.** Applying one supply model uniformly across a catalogue is a common mistake. The right model — dropshipping for new references, consignment for proven best-sellers, own stock for volume leaders — changes both your margin profile and your operational flexibility. The velocity data to make this decision exists in every e-commerce business; most do not use it systematically.

**SEO is an operating function with compounding returns.** The investment in content infrastructure, process, and tooling that gets you to 200k monthly visitors does not deliver immediate payback. It compounds over 18–24 months. Businesses that treat SEO as a campaign rather than a sustained operational investment consistently underperform on organic traffic.

**B2B signals in a B2C business are market data.** If professionals are buying a consumer product in volume, that is a message. Build for them deliberately — with the operational specificity that B2B service levels require.

---

## What came next

I left Ligerio in mid-2025, on good terms, with the company in a strong operational position. Jean de Varine continues to lead the business.

The experience at Ligerio directly shaped what I am building now at [Moverz](https://moverz.fr) — an AI-driven pricing and operations engine for the moving services market. A different industry, but structurally similar: a fragmented, high-complexity service market where most operators work manually and lack of transparency creates inefficiency for everyone. The winner will be the player who builds the best operational infrastructure first.

If you are building or scaling a business with genuine operational complexity — heavy logistics, supplier coordination, multi-channel operations, high average order values — I am available at [gdetaisne@gmail.com](mailto:gdetaisne@gmail.com) or on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/guillaume-stehelin-de-taisne-4a59805a/).

---

**Sources and further reading:**
- [Le Panier podcast #286 — Ligerio, 10M de CA en 5 ans en vendant des matériaux de construction](https://lepanier.io/10m-de-ca-en-5-ans-en-vendant-des-materiaux-de-construction/) — Laurent Kretz, CosaVostra (May 2024)
- [FrenchWeb — Ligerio raises €3.9M from Go Capital and BPI](https://www.frenchweb.fr/seed-e-commerce-ligerio-leve-39-millions-deuros-aupres-de-go-capital-et-de-business-angels/437388) (November 2022)
- [Clic Logistic — Ligerio case study](http://www.clic-logistic.com/case_study/ligerio/)

title: What Rocket Internet Taught Me About Execution — Launching 7 Companies in 8 Months in West Africa
excerpt: From 2013 to 2017, I operated across West Africa and Europe as a Finance & Operations executive for Africa Internet Group — the Rocket Internet entity that built Jumia. I incorporated 7 companies in Cameroon in 8 months, managed 60+ direct reports, and handled crises most finance executives only read about in case studies. Here is what that experience actually looked like.
content:
# What Rocket Internet Taught Me About Execution — Launching 7 Companies in 8 Months in West Africa

In 2013, Rocket Internet was the most talked-about company in European tech. The Samwer brothers were simultaneously building Amazon, eBay, Airbnb, and Instacart clones in 100+ countries with an organisational ruthlessness that Silicon Valley found both impressive and deeply uncomfortable. Oliver Samwer was famous for a single line that captured the entire philosophy: *"We are builders, not innovators. Someone else is the architect and we are the builders."*

I joined Africa Internet Group — the Rocket Internet vehicle building Jumia and six other vertical e-commerce brands across Africa — in 2013. Over five years, I operated in Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, and across West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Algeria), before finishing in Berlin for the sale of Glossybox to The Hut Group in 2017.

This is an article about what operating inside a Rocket Internet company actually looks and feels like — and what it taught me about finance, operations, and the limits of speed as a strategy.

---

## The Samwer doctrine: proven models, maximum speed, no excuses

Understanding Rocket Internet's operational culture requires understanding its founding logic. The brothers were not building startups in the Silicon Valley sense — organisations searching for product-market fit. They were building companies with *already validated* business models, transplanting them into markets where the model existed but no dominant local player had yet established itself.

Africa in 2012–2013 was a perfect storm for this approach. Internet penetration was growing fast, smartphone adoption was accelerating, and the largest consumer class in history was emerging on the continent — without a single dominant e-commerce player to serve it. Jumia launched in Nigeria in 2012 as the continent's first large-scale e-commerce platform, backed by Summit Partners ($26M in March 2013), then MTN, Millicom, and AXA, before a $150M round in November 2014 that expanded to nine African markets.

The operational model was standardised and aggressive. Every market launch followed the same sequence: incorporate a legal entity, hire a country managing director, stand up the core team (tech, logistics, commercial, finance, customer service), integrate with the central technology and logistics stack, and hit KPIs within 90 days. The KPIs were non-negotiable, the reporting was weekly, and the pressure was constant.

Speed was not just a preference — it was the core competitive hypothesis. If you move faster than any competitor can react, you capture the market before they can mobilise. If you capture the market, you own the network effects. If you own the network effects, you eventually win on unit economics. This logic held — until it didn't, but more on that later.

---

## Cameroon: 7 companies in 8 months

I arrived in Cameroon in 2013 to open the country's operations for Africa Internet Group. The mandate was to launch all of AIG's vertical brands simultaneously: Jumia (e-commerce), Jovago (travel), Lamudi (real estate), HelloFood (food delivery), Carmudi (automotive), and two others. In eight months, I incorporated seven legal entities.

To understand what that means in practice, you need to understand what company formation looks like in Cameroon. Historically, the process was described by local legal advisors as "a huge nightmare" — months, sometimes years, to legalise a business through a system marked by bureaucratic complexity and opacity. The government had launched enterprise creation one-stop-shops (CFCEs) to streamline the process, but effectiveness varied enormously by city and by the competence of the individuals you encountered on any given day.

What Rocket Internet gave you to cut through this was three things:

**1. A playbook.** Every AIG country launch had been done before somewhere else. There were templates for the legal structure, the shareholding, the bank account setup, the tax registration, the labour agreements. You were not solving a novel problem — you were executing a known protocol in an unfamiliar context.

**2. Capital.** Rocket's model was capital-intensive by design. You did not wait until you had revenue to invest in infrastructure. You built the infrastructure first, then drove revenue into it. This meant you could move faster than any local competitor who had to bootstrap.

**3. A network.** Every difficult local problem — a blocked tax registration, a landlord dispute, a regulatory barrier — had been encountered in some version by someone else in the AIG network. You could ask. And people answered, because the culture valued speed over ego.

What Rocket Internet did not give you was time. The pressure to open, hire, and hit KPIs was relentless. Building a company from zero to 100 people in months, in a country where infrastructure is fragile and bureaucratic friction is real, requires a specific kind of operational stamina. You are simultaneously a founder (deciding everything), a COO (hiring, building processes), a CFO (bank accounts, tax registrations, intercompany flows), and a country head (representing the company to suppliers, landlords, regulators, and the government).

By the end of those eight months, we had operating businesses across seven verticals, offices in Douala and Yaoundé, and teams hired, trained and reporting weekly to the AIG central team in Lagos.

---

## Côte d'Ivoire: scaling with a McKinsey-trained MD

After Cameroon, I moved to Côte d'Ivoire — the most structured and commercially developed of the francophone West African markets. I spent two years there, working alongside Francis Dufay, who joined as Co-Managing Director in April 2014 before becoming MD in 2015. (Francis later became CEO of Jumia group — one of the most consequential career trajectories to emerge from the AIG network.)

Côte d'Ivoire was a different operational context from Cameroon. The market was more mature, the commercial infrastructure was more developed, and Abidjan had the density of a genuine business hub. Jumia Côte d'Ivoire grew from 100 to 350 employees between mid-2014 and mid-2015, expanded to eight operational hubs across the country, and built a catalogue of 50,000 products with 500,000 monthly website visitors.

The operational challenge at this stage was different from the launch phase. You were no longer building from zero — you were scaling an operating business while simultaneously fixing the things that worked at 10 orders a day but broke at 100. Logistics routing. Return processes. Customer service resolution time. Supplier payment terms. Inventory accuracy.

In an AIG context, this happened under intense KPI scrutiny. Every week, country teams submitted standardised performance reports to the regional head office. Metrics were compared across markets. Countries that underperformed received attention; countries that outperformed received benchmarks that became the new floor. The system created genuine peer pressure across the portfolio — you knew exactly how you were performing relative to Nigeria, Kenya, and Morocco, and underperformance was visible to everyone.

This cross-market transparency was one of Rocket Internet's genuine operational innovations. Most companies at this scale would have had each country as a silo, with performance reviewed quarterly by a remote executive team. AIG had real-time data across 9+ markets and used it to drive urgency.

---

## What "crisis operations" actually looked like

The narrative about emerging market operations often focuses on macro risks: political instability, currency volatility, infrastructure failures. Those exist — but the crises I spent most of my time handling were more prosaic and more instructive.

**Executive fraud.** Several times across different markets, we discovered that local managing directors or senior team members were extracting cash from the business. This is not unique to Africa — it is a risk in any high-growth environment where controls are immature and growth pressure creates cover. The response protocol was always the same: protect the evidence, secure the accounts, remove access immediately, and put an interim CFO or controller in place within 48 hours while the investigation ran. Rocket Internet's network was useful here too — you could move a trusted operator from Lagos to Dakar within a week if you needed someone with institutional knowledge and a clean record.

**Tax audit crisis management.** In several markets, tax authority audits triggered the sudden departure of the local CFO — either because the exposure was larger than disclosed, or because the personal liability risk was real enough that individuals chose flight over resolution. The operational problem is not the tax audit itself — it is that you now have a country with an active audit, no CFO, and a team that is watching to see what the parent company does. The answer is to move fast, get a competent replacement in front of the tax authority within days, demonstrate cooperation and control, and simultaneously run a parallel assessment of the actual exposure. This is unglamorous work. It requires financial rigour, negotiation skills, and the ability to operate under pressure without showing it to the team.

**Planned social plans and labour negotiations.** As AIG consolidated its portfolio in 2016 — rebranding all subsidiaries under the Jumia name and restructuring several markets — some countries required significant workforce reductions. In markets with formal labour law and union representation, this means formal negotiation with works councils and, in some cases, the relevant ministry of labour. The process requires legal precision, communication discipline, and the ability to hold a dual mandate: protect the company's financial position while treating departing employees with genuine respect. Botching this creates reputational damage that outlasts the savings.

None of these situations are in the MBA curriculum. They require a combination of financial rigour, operational speed, interpersonal judgment, and political awareness that you only develop by doing it.

---

## The SWAT year: Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Algeria

After Côte d'Ivoire, I moved into what I would describe as a regional SWAT role — operating across Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, and Algeria to address specific operational problems that the local teams could not resolve alone.

Nigeria was the centrepiece of AIG's Africa story — the largest market, the most funding, and the most scrutiny. It was also the most operationally complex: logistics in Lagos required building a last-mile delivery network from scratch in one of the world's most congested cities, currency controls created FX management challenges, and the sheer scale of the operation meant that system failures had immediate and visible impact on revenue.

Ghana and Senegal were more contained but had their own specific challenges: smaller markets with less developed logistics infrastructure, more price-sensitive consumers, and the ongoing challenge of competing with the informal retail sector on price while delivering a premium service experience.

Algeria was notable for regulatory complexity — the country's import regime, banking system, and e-commerce regulations created a structural constraint on the business model that required creative adaptation. The Rocket Internet playbook did not transfer cleanly to markets with significant state intervention in commerce.

What this year taught me was the value of the outsider's eye. When you arrive in a market without the emotional investment of someone who has been there for two years, you see problems more clearly. You are not defending previous decisions. You can ask "why does this work this way?" without it being a challenge to anyone's identity. Good crisis operators are good partly because of competence, and partly because of the freedom that comes with having nothing to protect.

---

## Berlin and Glossybox: unblocking a sale that should not have been blocked

My final chapter with Rocket Internet was not a standard assignment. I was sent to Berlin because the Glossybox sale to The Hut Group was stuck — and the reason it was stuck was the accounting.

Glossybox was a genuinely differentiated Rocket Internet company. Founded in 2011 in Berlin, it was Europe's leading beauty subscription box — operating across France, Germany, the UK, the US, Sweden, Norway, and Austria — with a product that had real brand equity rather than simply replicating a proven model in a new market. The deal with THG was strategically sound. But it could not close.

The issue was the group's financial statements. Each of the seven entities across France, Germany, the US, Sweden, Norway, the UK, and Austria had been producing accounts under a patchwork of local accounting standards. None of them were IFRS-compliant in a form that a sophisticated buyer's due diligence team could stand behind. Working capital valuation methodologies were inconsistent across entities — which in a subscription business with deferred revenue, prepaid contracts, and complex accruals creates meaningful disagreements about what the business is actually worth. When a buyer cannot agree with a seller on what working capital is, deals do not close.

What made this structurally harder was the tax problem. Despite annual KPMG statutory audits across all entities, the Glossybox group had been incorrectly declaring its revenue since incorporation — in every market. The treatment of subscription revenue, gift box revenue, and B2B brand partnerships had not been consistently applied to local tax rules in each jurisdiction. When this was identified in the context of the sale process, the liability exposure across seven countries ran to eight figures. This is the kind of number that terminates acquisition conversations.

My mandate was to fix this so the deal could close:

**IFRS restatement across 7 entities.** We restated the financials for each country subsidiary to IFRS — harmonising revenue recognition, working capital policies, deferred income treatment, and intercompany eliminations. This required working simultaneously with local accountants in each market, aligning them to a common methodology, and producing a consolidated group view that a buyer's financial advisor could rely on.

**Working capital normalisation.** In M&A, working capital is typically one of the most contentious items in a deal — because it determines the final price adjustment at completion. In a subscription business, defining "normalised" working capital requires agreeing on how to treat prepaid subscriptions, deferred box delivery costs, and B2B contract accruals. We built a working capital model that was consistent across all entities and defensible under scrutiny.

**Tax regularisation.** For the revenue declaration errors, we worked with local tax advisors in each country to quantify the exposure, prepare voluntary disclosure packages where appropriate, and negotiate payment plans. You cannot sell a company with a live seven-figure, seven-country tax liability without a clear resolution path. The work was methodical, jurisdiction by jurisdiction, and required significant negotiation with tax authorities who were not expecting to receive a voluntary disclosure from a company they were not currently auditing.

**Data room preparation under live deal pressure.** All of this happened while the deal was actively ongoing — with a buyer team asking questions, an investment bank managing timelines, and a board that needed regular progress updates. The discipline of running financial remediation and vendor due diligence simultaneously, without letting either suffer, is genuinely hard. It requires a very clear separation of workstreams and a team that can hold both tracks in parallel.

The sale to THG closed in August 2017. THG planned to leverage its proprietary e-commerce technology platform and use Berlin as a European tech hub. The deal value was not disclosed.

What the Glossybox experience taught me is that the quality of financial infrastructure compounds silently. Seven years of inconsistent accounting across seven entities — each passing annual statutory audits — created a problem that nearly killed a strategically sound transaction. The auditors were checking for compliance with local GAAP. No one was building the group-level IFRS view. No one was stress-testing the tax treatment across jurisdictions. These are not exotic failures. They are common ones in any organisation that has grown faster than its finance function.

---

## What five years inside Rocket Internet gave me

Looking back, the most valuable thing I took from the Rocket Internet experience was not knowledge of any particular market or industry. It was a set of operating reflexes that only develop in extreme environments.

**Speed without chaos is a skill.** Rocket Internet moved fast, but the companies that survived were not the ones that moved fastest — they were the ones that moved fast while building real infrastructure. The companies that imploded did so because speed became a substitute for quality rather than a complement to it.

**Finance is a control function before it is a reporting function.** In every crisis I handled — embezzlement, tax audit, social plan — the underlying failure was a control failure. The reporting looked fine because the controls were not there to catch what was actually happening. Good finance leadership is not about closing the books on time. It is about knowing what is actually in them.

**Cross-market benchmarking is one of the most underused management tools.** The weekly KPI comparison across AIG's nine markets was uncomfortable and occasionally unfair — every market has specific conditions. But the discipline of knowing exactly how you compared to peers, in real time, created a level of urgency and accountability that no quarterly review process can replicate.

**Operating in fragile environments builds judgment.** When systems are robust, decisions are easy — the process tells you what to do. When systems are fragile or absent, you have to decide. The practice of deciding — quickly, with incomplete information, in high-stakes contexts — is the most valuable form of management education I know.

**Exit processes are operations, not events.** The Glossybox sale taught me that every transaction has an operational dimension that is just as important as the financial one. Due diligence is a process. Data room management is a process. Team communication during a sale is a process. The companies that get the best outcomes from exits are the ones that treat the transaction as an operational project, not a financial one.

**Clean is not always the goal. Aware is.** This is perhaps the hardest lesson, and the one most finance leaders get wrong. A perfectly clean business that does not execute is worth less than a messy one that grows. The CFO's job is not to eliminate all risk — it is to locate it, size it, and make an explicit decision about tolerance. In a high-growth environment, some problems should be fixed immediately. Others should be monitored. Others should be accepted as the cost of moving. The failure is not having imperfect financials or unresolved operational issues — that is the normal condition of any company moving fast. The failure is not knowing where the problems are. You can tolerate almost anything you have mapped. What kills businesses is the risk they have not identified.

This is where the Glossybox situation was genuinely instructive. The tax issue was not the result of deliberate evasion. It was the result of a finance function that was optimised for local statutory compliance and never stepped back to look at the group-level picture. No one had asked: does our revenue recognition methodology hold across all seven jurisdictions simultaneously? No one had built the cross-entity view. The problems were discoverable — they simply had not been discovered, because no one had looked. A good CFO looks. And then decides what to do about what they find.

---

## Further reading

- [TechCrunch — Jumia raises $150M, expands to 9 African markets](https://techcrunch.com/2014/11/26/rocket-internet-backed-jumia-raises-150m-for-its-african-e-commerce-business/) (November 2014)
- [Reuters — THG acquires Glossybox from Rocket Internet](https://www.reuters.com/article/the-hut-group-acquires-glossybox-from-ri-idUSL8N1L0311/) (August 2017)

content:
# Why C-level executives can’t perform anymore without deeply understanding technology

For years, senior executives could be excellent without really understanding technology. Finance owned the numbers, operations owned the teams, and “IT” owned the tools. That world is gone. Today, products are often software, distribution is digital, data is everywhere and AI is starting to rewrite value chains. In this context, a C-level who doesn’t understand tech in depth becomes a bottleneck – even if they are brilliant on the P&L.

According to McKinsey, **around 70% of digital transformations fail** to deliver the expected value, often due to a lack of real sponsorship and digital skills at the top. Research from the MIT Center for Information Systems Research shows that companies whose boards are “digitally savvy” enjoy **30–40% higher revenue growth and value creation** than their peers. In other words, technological competence at leadership and board level is no longer a bonus – it is a measurable performance driver.

---

## 1. Without tech literacy, leaders are flying blind

Not understanding tech today is not just about “not knowing how to code”. It means being blind to three fundamental dimensions of leadership: how systems really work, how reliable the data is, and where the real risks lie. When a C-level doesn’t understand how their systems work, they depend on internal “translators” for everything: why a KPI is moving, why a project takes six months instead of six weeks, why teams insist on a rebuild instead of another feature. This gap is costly: slower decisions, biased trade-offs, poorly framed projects.

A leader without tech literacy sees only the screens, not the flows behind them. They discuss KPIs without understanding how they are constructed, AI without seeing the training data, security without visualising the attack surface. As the organisation grows, the time needed to “understand what is really going on” explodes – and tech teams quietly learn to work around the top management instead of with it.

- **Without understanding systems**, a leader sees only interfaces, not dependencies (what talks to what, where data is lost, where costs explode).
- **Without understanding data**, they make decisions on top of reporting whose limits they can’t see (lag, bias, missing history, hand-rebuilt series).
- **Without understanding architectures**, they underestimate the real cost of change (necessary refactors, technical debt, security, team bandwidth).
- **Without understanding realistic AI use cases**, they either overhype or underuse it: gadgets and PoCs on one side, irrecoverable lag on the other.

This is exactly what Harvard Business Review and MIT Sloan keep pointing out: leaders who don’t understand technology depend more on internal narratives than on system reality – and their strategic decisions suffer.

---

## 2. What “deeply understanding technology” really means (and doesn’t)

We often confuse two notions: **being a CTO** and **being a tech-savvy C-level**. A CFO, COO or CEO doesn’t need to become a cloud architect, but they can no longer afford to have only a superficial view. The goal is not to write every line of code; it is to think in systems, challenge technical choices and understand orders of magnitude for cost and risk.

For a C-level, “deeply understanding technology” means very concrete things:

- **Thinking in systems**: being able to mentally map flows (customers → product → invoicing → cash), dependencies (CRM, line-of-business tools, ERP, bank, BI) and friction points. Being able to ask: *“If we change this here, what breaks over there?”*.
- **Understanding the main technical building blocks**: without going into code, knowing what monoliths, microservices, APIs, data warehouses, integrations and AI models imply. Not to build them, but to understand their cost, rigidity and speed of evolution.
- **Reading data with intelligent scepticism**: asking the right questions: where does this data come from? How often is it updated? What don’t we see? What is the realistic error range? Many governance failures stem from leaders who don’t know how to spot weak signals in their systems.
- **Understanding genuine AI productivity levers**: distinguishing between use cases where AI is structurally meaningful (back-office automation, classification, forecasting, internal copilots) and those where it is still a gadget. Knowing what this requires in terms of data, security and change management.

Schools like Harvard, Stanford or CentraleSupélec increasingly emphasise this hybrid competence in their executive programmes: not to turn CxOs into developers, but into **decision architects** able to talk eye-to-eye with tech teams.

---

## 3. Why this is critical for CFOs and COOs in particular

For a CFO or COO, technology is not just another topic. It **is** the connective tissue of finance and operations: what makes numbers land on time, teams know what to do and customers experience a consistent journey. A CFO/COO without tech literacy is, by design, behind what is really happening in the business.

When a CFO/COO doesn’t master tech, reporting is slow, fragile and patched together; teams spend their time reconciling spreadsheets instead of running the business; IT projects are seen as “costs” rather than structural changes. A tech-savvy CFO/COO, on the contrary, can play a very different role.

- **Designing a genuine operating system for the company**: a backbone tying together CRM, orders, inventory, invoicing, treasury, accounting and support. When this backbone is well designed, numbers “come up on their own”, alerts are automated and decisions rely on live data.
- **Massively automating low-value work**: bank reconciliation, invoice chasing, margin checks are perfect candidates for workflow + AI. A tech-savvy CFO/COO doesn’t just ask for “a tool”: they can specify rules, required data and exceptions.
- **Redefining internal roles**: instead of stacking layers of middle-management and back-office, they redesign roles around decisions and exceptions, while letting the system handle routines. This is exactly the promise of projects like Moverz: delivering the service level of a profitable 50-person company… with no employees, powered by systems.
- **Speaking the language of investors and family offices**: the most advanced funds know that value lies in systems. A CFO/COO able to clearly explain architecture, data, AI and automation levers reassures not only on the P&L but on operational resilience.

World Economic Forum data is clear: by 2027, **around 60% of workers will need significant reskilling**, with digital and analytical skills consistently at the top of the list. If finance and ops leadership is not ahead of this curve, it will inevitably lag behind its own organisation.

---

## 4. What research says (Harvard, MIT, McKinsey, WEF…)

Several streams of research converge on one point: **organisations with digitally savvy leaders outperform others**. This is now documented beyond anecdotes, with numbers.

- **MIT CISR – digital boards**: companies whose boards include several digitally savvy members show 30–40% higher revenue growth and value creation than their peers, with stronger margins.
- **McKinsey – digital transformation failure**: in “Unlocking success in digital transformations”, McKinsey notes that around 70% of digital transformations fail to create the expected value. Success factors include strong top-management involvement, a willingness to rethink operating models, and investment in digital skills at leadership level.
- **Harvard / Stanford – leadership and disruption**: Harvard Business Review and Stanford’s Technology Ventures Program underline that leaders who understand disruptive technologies (cloud, data, AI) are the ones who manage to transform their organisations without breaking them: they know where to experiment, where to industrialise, and where not to touch.
- **World Economic Forum – skills of the future**: the WEF shows that analytical thinking, digital literacy and understanding of AI are among the most requested skills for leaders – not as cosmetic “nice-to-haves”, but as core abilities to redesign work and value chains.

All these sources point in the same direction: technology is no longer a support function; it is a language. Leaders who don’t speak that language increasingly depend on those who do – internally or at competitors.

---

## 5. How a C-level can realistically become tech-savvy

The good news is that this competence **can be learned**, even for profiles strongly oriented towards finance, operations or strategy. It is less a matter of age than of exposure, discipline and intellectual humility. More and more executives are going “back to school”, through executive programmes or deeper degrees.

A few concrete levers for a C-level:

- **Take a structured programme, not just attend conferences**: executive education at Harvard, Stanford, MIT, CentraleSupélec… or, as I do, a Computer Science degree at Harvard. The idea is not to collect certificates, but to confront the rigour of the discipline (algorithms, data, systems).
- **Work on real products and tools, not just mock-ups**: co-designing or even coding internal tools (even simple ones) changes how you think. You see what is trivial, what is complex, what is expensive, what is fragile. A C-level who has deployed an internal tool or automation end-to-end never looks at IT projects the same way.
- **Spend time inside systems with tech/data teams**: instead of consuming only PowerPoint summaries, sit with developers and data engineers, look at raw dashboards, logs and architecture diagrams. Ask naïve questions, and accept not understanding everything at first.
- **Index leadership practice on technology**: for each strategic decision (new country, new product, M&A, cost cutting), systematically ask: which systems does this impact? What data is needed to steer this decision? Which part of this decision can be augmented by AI or automation?

The logic is simple: the more a C-level is exposed to system reality, the less dependent they are on technical storytelling – and the faster and sharper their decisions become.

---

## 6. Towards “full-stack” C-levels: finance, ops, tech, AI

We often talk about “full-stack” developers. But the real challenge for the coming years is **“full-stack” C-levels**: executives able, in the same meeting, to move from a gross-margin issue to a data-schema question, from an architecture dilemma to a cost-reduction plan, from a product detail to a board discussion.

A CFO/COO who:

- has operated in extreme contexts (Jumia, Glossybox, Ligerio…);
- can build or specify systems themselves (TypeScript, AI, automation);
- and deepens this competence through a Computer Science curriculum at Harvard;

sends a very clear signal to the market: **“I don’t lead by gut feeling, I lead through systems.”**

For funded scale-ups and family offices, this is exactly the profile that makes the difference: someone who can take over in a crisis *and* **design the machine** that will prevent the same crisis from happening again – finance, operations, tech and AI in the same head.

---

## Further reading

- **Harvard Law School – Corporate Governance Forum**: *How board and C-suite collaboration can build organizational resilience*  
  https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2025/10/22/how-board-and-c-suite-collaboration-can-build-organizational-resilience/
- **Stanford Technology Ventures Program** – Leadership and disruptive technologies  
  https://stvp.stanford.edu/videos/leadership-and-disruptive-technologies-entire-talk/transcript-pdf-leadership-and-disruptive-technologies-entire-talk
- **World Economic Forum – Future of Jobs Report** (latest edition)  
  https://www.weforum.org/reports/the-future-of-jobs-report-2023/
- **CentraleSupélec – Computer science programmes for engineers and leaders**  
  https://www.centralesupelec.fr/programmes/ingenieur-specialite-informatique
